subject: Mathematics
title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
summary: Trigonometric functions are not one-one, so their inverses are defined on restricted intervals called principal value branches.
sin⁻¹x and tan⁻¹x take values in [−π/2, π/2] (tan⁻¹ open); cos⁻¹x and cot⁻¹x in [0, π]. Know each domain and range exactly.
Key identities: sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2, tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)) when xy < 1, and the 2tan⁻¹x conversions.
Most JEE questions test sin⁻¹(sin x)-type expressions outside the principal branch — draw the graph or shift by π.

formulas.name: Negative arguments
formulas.formula: sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹x;  tan⁻¹(−x) = −tan⁻¹x;  cosec⁻¹(−x) = −cosec⁻¹x;  cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x;  cot⁻¹(−x) = π − cot⁻¹x;  sec⁻¹(−x) = π − sec⁻¹x

formulas.name: Complementary pairs
formulas.formula: sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2;  tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2;  sec⁻¹x + cosec⁻¹x = π/2

formulas.name: Reciprocal relations
formulas.formula: sin⁻¹(1/x) = cosec⁻¹x;  cos⁻¹(1/x) = sec⁻¹x;  tan⁻¹(1/x) = cot⁻¹x (x > 0), = cot⁻¹x − π (x < 0)

formulas.name: Sum of tan⁻¹
formulas.formula: tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)) if xy < 1;  = π + tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)) if x, y > 0 and xy > 1
formulas.mistake: Check xy < 1 before using the plain formula.

formulas.name: sin⁻¹(sin x) outside branch
formulas.formula: sin⁻¹(sin x) = x on [−π/2, π/2];  = π − x on [π/2, 3π/2];  = x − 2π on [3π/2, 5π/2]

formulas.name: cos⁻¹(cos x) outside branch
formulas.formula: cos⁻¹(cos x) = x on [0, π];  = 2π − x on [π, 2π]
formulas.when: Graph is a zig-zag starting at the origin.

formulas.name: Converting one function to another
formulas.formula: sin⁻¹x = cos⁻¹√(1 − x²) = tan⁻¹(x/√(1 − x²)) for 0 ≤ x < 1
formulas.when: Draw a right triangle with opposite x, hypotenuse 1.

examples.title: Principal value
examples.solution: 150° is outside [−90°, 90°]; sin 150° = sin 30°, so the answer is 30° = π/6 (computed 30°).

examples.title: cos(tan⁻¹ ¾)
examples.solution: Triangle with opposite 3, adjacent 4, hypotenuse 5 ⇒ cos = 4/5 = 0.8.

examples.title: Outside the branch
examples.solution: 4π/3 lies in [π/2, 3π/2], so sin⁻¹(sin x) = π − x = π − 4π/3 = −π/3.

examples.title: Sum equals π
examples.solution: tan⁻¹2 + tan⁻¹3 = π + tan⁻¹((2 + 3)/(1 − 6)) = π + tan⁻¹(−1) = π − π/4 (since xy > 1). Adding tan⁻¹1 = π/4 gives π.

examples.title: Telescoping sum
examples.problem: Find Σ (r = 1 to n) tan⁻¹(1/(1 + r + r²)).
examples.solution: Each term = tan⁻¹(r + 1) − tan⁻¹r, so the sum telescopes to tan⁻¹(n + 1) − tan⁻¹1 = tan⁻¹(n + 1) − π/4.

topics.title: Why branches are needed
topics.explain: A function has an inverse only if it is one-one and onto. Restricting sin x to [−π/2, π/2] makes it a bijection onto [−1, 1]; other branches like [π/2, 3π/2] are possible but the principal branch is standard.

topics.title: Graphs
topics.explain: y = sin⁻¹x rises from (−1, −π/2) to (1, π/2); y = cos⁻¹x falls from (−1, π) to (1, 0); y = tan⁻¹x has horizontal asymptotes y = ±π/2. Graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in y = x.

topics.title: sin(sin⁻¹x) vs sin⁻¹(sin x)
topics.explain: sin(sin⁻¹x) = x for all x in [−1, 1] (always true in its domain). sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only when x is in the principal branch.

topics.title: Substitution technique
topics.explain: Expressions like √(1 − x²), (1 − x²)/(1 + x²), 2x/(1 − x²) suggest x = sin θ, cos θ or tan θ; then simplify and convert back, keeping track of the branch.

topics.title: Solving equations
topics.explain: Convert everything to one inverse function, use identities, then take sin, cos or tan of both sides. Always check that the final answers lie in the domains.

topics.title: Common traps
topics.explain: tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹(1/x) = π/2 only for x > 0 (it is −π/2 for x < 0). cos⁻¹x is never negative. sec⁻¹ and cosec⁻¹ are undefined for |x| < 1. Writing sin⁻¹x as 1/sin x is wrong — it is an inverse, not a reciprocal.

ratta: sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹ → [−π/2, π/2];  cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹ → [0, π].
tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)), xy < 1.
